When studied under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the reproductive biology of the Northern pygmy mouse (Baiomys taylori) reveals several tightly constrained life-history parameters. Gestation in this diminutive rodent lasts precisely 20 days [tg = 20 days], a relatively short period that is consistent with its small body size and rapid life cycle at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Females typically produce litters containing 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 pups per litter], and the frequency of these reproductive events is such that the maximum reproductive rate approximates 10 litters per year [F_R_i = 10 litters per year]. This combination of moderate litter size and relatively frequent breeding cycles allows the species to achieve substantial annual recruitment despite its modest adult body mass. The gestation period, measured as the interval from copulation through embryogenesis to parturition, is brief enough to permit multiple reproductive attempts within a single breeding season, a strategy that is advantageous in the unpredictable environments of their grassland and scrubland habitats across the southern United States and Mexico.

Neonatal body mass at the moment of live birth is remarkably low, a trait that reflects the altricial developmental mode typical of many murid rodents. Newborn pups emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 1.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.2 grams], making them among the smallest rodent neonates relative to adult size. This altricial state is typical of murid rodents, and the newborn offspring are entirely dependent upon the lactating female for warmth and nourishment. The period of dependency is relatively brief, however, and rapid growth ensues during the suckling stage. Following the onset of lactation and a period of intensive nursing, the milk-dependent young undergo a dietary transition to solid foods. Weaning, marking the end of maternal milk provisioning, occurs at 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth], which is the point at which the suckling juveniles achieve nutritional independence from the dam at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At this weaning age, the offspring have grown considerably from their neonatal mass.

The wet weight of the young at the time of weaning has been recorded as 3.6 grams [Wwx = 3.6 grams], representing a threefold increase over the birth mass achieved in just three weeks of intensive nursing under conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This rapid mass gain is fueled by the high lipid content of the mother's milk and reflects the intense metabolic demands placed upon both the lactating female and the developing pups. Following weaning, the young enter a juvenile and sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth toward the ultimate adult body mass. The maximum adult wet weight attained by fully grown, reproductively mature individuals in captivity reaches 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], a figure that underscores the species' status as one of the smallest extant rodents in North America. This adult size is achieved after several weeks of post-weaning growth, during which the weaned juveniles forage independently for seeds and insects.

The progression toward reproductive maturation in Baiomys taylori exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing when animals are maintained under standard laboratory husbandry conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Females attain puberty, marked by the first vaginal opening and the onset of the initial oestrous cycle, at 44 days after birth [tp = 44 days after birth] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. In contrast, males require a longer developmental period before achieving reproductive maturity, with the first spermatozoa appearing in the epididymides at 75 days after birth [tp = 75 days after birth] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This disparity in the time since birth at puberty between the sexes is a common pattern in many rodent species, and it may be linked to the differential energetic costs associated with gametogenesis and the establishment of territorial behavior in males. The earlier maturation of females allows them to begin breeding sooner, which is advantageous in short-lived species with high annual reproductive turnover.

Longevity data for the Northern pygmy mouse, gathered from captive colony records at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 1,205 days [am = approximately 1,205 days], which translates to roughly 3.3 years. This lifespan is modest even by rodent standards, yet it is typical for a species with such a high metabolic rate and small body size. The 1,205-day figure represents the oldest documented individual in a carefully monitored colony. Natural mortality in the wild likely occurs considerably earlier due to predation, food scarcity, and environmental stressors, though the underlying physiological process of senescence presumably follows a similar trajectory. The fast pace of the life history in Baiomys taylori, characterized by a brief gestation and rapid juvenile growth accelerating toward early female reproduction, is well-suited to the ephemeral grassland habitats it occupies across its geographic range.
